subtitle: Identify a person's cultural needs without guessing from their background, find and offer culturally responsive providers, and record and follow through on what you learn, as Minnesota's informed decision-making law asks.
audience: For assessors, case managers and support planners who work with people using disability waiver services. It explains the law's expectations in plain terms and does not replace DHS guidance, lead agency policy or legal advice.

lessons.title: What the law asks, and why it matters
objectives: Describe informed choice and informed decision making as Minnesota law uses them for disability services.
Quote the part of Minnesota Statutes 256B.4905, subdivision 3a, that names cultural needs.
Explain why cultural needs are part of making a real choice, not an extra.
Recognize when a cultural needs question is being treated as a checkbox.
lessons.teaching:
Minnesota's policy for home and community-based services, in Minnesota Statutes, section 256B.4905, says people with disabilities should be able to make informed choices about their services. An informed choice depends on the person having, in a way that fits their needs, the tools, information and opportunities to understand all their options.

For people using waiver services, subdivision 3a describes informed decision making, the process that supports that choice. Among the things it must address is "identification of the person's cultural needs and access to culturally responsive services and providers." It sits alongside the person's own preferences and goals, accommodations they need, all available options, visits, peers and enough time to decide.

Culture is in the law because it changes what a good choice looks like. A provider can be excellent and still be the wrong fit if no one speaks the person's language, if staff cannot honor their faith practices or diet, or if the person's family expects to be part of decisions and the provider shuts them out. A choice made without those things in view is a choice between options that may not really be available to that person.

The risk is that this becomes a checkbox. A field marked "cultural needs: none" usually means nobody asked well, not that the person has none. Everyone has a culture: a language, family roles, routines, beliefs, foods, holidays, ways of talking about disability. The question is which of those matter for their services, and only the person and those close to them can answer that.
lessons.keyPoint: Minnesota law makes cultural needs part of informed decision making. A blank or "none" usually means nobody asked well.
lessons.example: Practice case: The assessor notices that most plans on the team list "cultural needs: none identified." Asked about it, a colleague says the question feels awkward, so they usually skip it unless the person brings something up.
lessons.question: What should the assessor suggest to the team?
choices: Keep skipping it, since people will mention anything important.
Fill in cultural needs based on each person's background, to save time.
Agree on two or three open, respectful ways to ask about what matters to the person, and try them for a month.
feedback: Many people will not raise these needs with an agency unless asked. Skipping the question can leave real needs out of the plan.
Guessing from background is stereotyping. Two people from the same community can have very different needs.
This makes the question easier to ask and treats it as part of informed decision making, as the law expects.
lessons.reflection: Which parts of your own culture would matter to you if someone came into your home to help every day?
lessons.action: Look at three plans you have written or reviewed recently. Note how cultural needs were recorded, and whether the words came from the person.

check.question: What does Minnesota Statutes 256B.4905, subdivision 3a, say informed decision making must include about culture?
check.correct: Identification of the person's cultural needs and access to culturally responsive services and providers.
wrong: A record of the person's race and ethnicity.
A provider from the same community as the person.
check.feedback: The law names cultural needs and access to culturally responsive services and providers. It does not reduce culture to a demographic field or require a provider from any particular community.

lessons.title: Asking about cultural needs without guessing
objectives: Ask open questions about what matters to the person in daily life and care.
Avoid assuming a person's needs from their name, language or community.
Include the people the person wants involved in decisions, at the person's choice.
Use the National CLAS Standards' principal standard as a guide for respectful, understandable services.
lessons.teaching:
Asking about cultural needs well starts with curiosity, not a list of facts about groups. Two people from the same community can differ completely in language, faith, family roles and what they want from services. Background can suggest a question to ask. It never answers it.

Open questions work better than labels. What is important to you in how people help you at home? Is there anything about your faith, your food or your routines that helpers should know? Who do you like to have with you when decisions are made? Are there things a helper could do that would make you uncomfortable? Is there a language you are most comfortable in? These questions let the person tell you what matters, in their words.

Family and community roles deserve care. In some families, decisions are made together, and leaving relatives out would feel disrespectful. In others, the person wants more independence than their family expects. Ask the person who they want involved, and respect their answer. The choice of services is theirs.

The National Standards for Culturally and Linguistically Appropriate Services, known as the National CLAS Standards, are published by the federal Office of Minority Health. Their principal standard begins: "Provide effective, understandable, and respectful quality care and services." That is a useful test for any question you ask about culture. Is it respectful? Will the person understand why you are asking? Will the answer change their services for the better?
lessons.keyPoint: Ask what matters, in open questions and in the person's own words. Background can suggest a question; it never answers it.
lessons.example: Practice case: Preparing for a planning meeting, the newer colleague tells the case manager, "The family is from a community where women always handle care at home, so I'll note that the mother is the main helper."
lessons.question: What should the case manager say?
choices: "Good idea, that will save time in the meeting."
"Let's ask the family who helps and who they want involved. Each family is different."
"Leave family roles out of the plan entirely, so we don't make assumptions."
feedback: This records an assumption about a whole community as a fact about one family, and it may be wrong.
This turns a guess into a question, so the plan reflects this family, in their words.
Avoiding assumptions is right, but leaving family roles out can miss real needs. Ask instead of guessing or ignoring.
lessons.reflection: When have you made an assumption about someone based on their background that turned out to be wrong? What did you learn?
lessons.action: Write three open questions about cultural needs that you are comfortable asking. Use at least one in your next assessment or planning meeting.

check.question: Which is the best way to learn a person's cultural needs?
check.correct: Ask open questions about what matters to them, and record their answers in their own words.
wrong: Look up common practices for their community and apply them.
Assume needs are the same as the last person you served from that community.
check.feedback: Community information can help you know what to ask about, but only the person can say what applies to them. Recording their own words keeps the plan accurate.

lessons.title: Finding and offering culturally responsive providers
objectives: Describe what makes a provider culturally responsive for a particular person.
Ask providers specific questions about language, practices and flexibility.
Use navigators, community organizations and Disability Hub MN to widen the search.
Respond honestly when no responsive provider is available, and record the gap.
lessons.teaching:
A culturally responsive provider is not defined by a label on a website. It is a provider that can meet this person's needs: staff who speak their language or work well with interpreters, practices that respect their faith, food and routines, a willingness to include family the way the person wants and a willingness to adapt.

Ask providers specific questions, based on what the person told you. Do you have staff who speak this language? How do you handle prayer times, dietary needs or a preference for a helper of a particular gender? How would you include the person's family in decisions? What would you change to make this work? A provider's answers, and how they answer, tell you a lot.

Widen the search beyond the usual list. Navigators and community organizations often know providers that serve their community well. Disability Hub MN, a free statewide resource network, can help people and families find information and resources. Bring what you find back to the person, and let them choose.

Sometimes no responsive provider is available, especially outside the metro area or for smaller language communities. Say so honestly. Then look at what can be done: a provider willing to train or adapt, interpreter support or a different service arrangement the person's program allows. Record what was looked for and what was not found. That record matters to the person, and it shows the program where the gaps are.
lessons.keyPoint: A responsive provider meets this person's needs. Ask specific questions, widen the search and record gaps honestly when nothing fits.
lessons.example: Practice case: The person wants a home care provider whose staff speak their language. The case manager finds none in the county and tells the navigator there is nothing to be done.
lessons.question: What is the best next step?
choices: Ask the navigator and community organizations what they know, ask likely providers what they could adapt, bring the options to the person and record any gap.
Offer the first available provider and close the question.
Put services on hold until a provider who speaks the language is found.
feedback: This widens the search, asks what is possible and leaves the choice with the person, while recording the gap for the program.
This gets services started but may ignore a need the person named. They may not realize other options exist.
Holding services can leave the person without help. The person should decide whether to wait or start with the best available option.
lessons.reflection: Where do you usually look for providers? Who might know about options you have never seen?
lessons.action: Write four specific questions you would ask a provider about meeting a person's cultural needs. Keep them for your next search.

check.question: No provider in the area meets a person's language need. What should happen?
check.correct: Tell the person honestly, explore what providers could adapt and record what was looked for and not found.
wrong: Record the language need as met, since there was no other choice.
Remove the language need from the plan so it does not appear unmet.
check.feedback: An honest record helps the person and shows the program where gaps are. Hiding the gap, or recording it as met, keeps it from ever being fixed.

lessons.title: Recording it, and following through
objectives: Record cultural needs specifically and in the person's own words.
Document the options discussed, as the law expects.
Revisit cultural needs when life or services change.
Pass patterns of unmet needs to someone who can address them.
lessons.teaching:
A good record makes the next conversation easier. Write cultural needs specifically and, where you can, in the person's words. "Prefers family care" says very little. "Wants their sister present when care decisions are made; prefers a female helper for bathing; needs time for prayer before noon" tells the next worker what to do.

Minnesota's informed choice policy also expects documentation, in a manner the commissioner prescribes, of each option discussed. Recording the options you offered, and why the person chose as they did, protects the person and shows that the choice was real. It also helps when the person's situation changes and the choice needs another look.

Cultural needs are not fixed. A person's language needs can change after a stroke. Family roles shift when a parent ages. A person may become more or less connected to their faith community. Ask again at renewals and whenever services change, rather than copying last year's answer forward.

Finally, look up from the single case. When you keep seeing the same unmet need, such as no providers who speak a language, or providers unable to meet a common dietary need, pass that pattern to your supervisor or program manager. One record is a person's story. A pattern is information the program can act on.
lessons.keyPoint: Record cultural needs specifically and in the person's words, document the options discussed, ask again when things change and pass patterns on.
lessons.example: Practice case: Reviewing plans, the supervisor finds one that says only "cultural needs: prefers family." The assessor who wrote it remembers that the person talked about wanting their sister present for decisions and a female helper for personal care.
lessons.question: What should the supervisor ask the assessor to do?
choices: Leave it, since the gist is captured.
Delete the note, since it is too vague to use.
Update the plan with the specific needs the person described, in their words, and check them with the person at the next contact.
feedback: The gist is not enough for a helper who has never met the person. Specific needs are what change the care.
Deleting the note loses information. Making it specific is better than removing it.
This turns a vague note into guidance a helper can follow, and checks it with the person rather than relying on memory alone.
lessons.reflection: If a new worker read your last plan with no other information, would they know what matters most to the person?
lessons.action: Choose one plan and rewrite its cultural needs section in specific, plain words. Check the new version with the person at your next contact.

check.question: Why record the options discussed with a person, not only the option chosen?
check.correct: It shows the choice was informed, follows the state's informed choice policy and helps when the choice needs another look.
wrong: So the person cannot change their mind later.
It is only needed when the person refuses services.
check.feedback: Minnesota's informed choice policy expects documentation of each option discussed. The record supports the person's choice and makes it easier to revisit, not harder.

cards.back: A choice the person makes with the tools, information and opportunities they need to understand all their options.
Minn. Stat. 256B.4905, subd. 3a: "identification of the person's cultural needs and access to culturally responsive services and providers."
Background can suggest a question. Only the person can answer it.
One that can meet this person's needs: language, practices, family involvement and willingness to adapt.
Federal standards whose principal standard begins: "Provide effective, understandable, and respectful quality care and services."
Write needs in the person's words, document options discussed and ask again when life changes.

aid.heading: Ask
items: What is important to you in how people help you?
Anything about your faith, food or routines helpers should know?
Who do you want with you when decisions are made?
Which language are you most comfortable in?

aid.heading: Find
items: Ask providers specific questions about language, practices and family involvement.
Ask navigators and community organizations what they know.
Point families to Disability Hub MN for free help with resources.
Bring the options back to the person to choose.

aid.heading: Record
items: Write cultural needs specifically, in the person's words.
Document each option discussed and why the person chose.
Record what was looked for and not found.

aid.heading: Follow through
items: Ask again at renewals and when services change.
Pass patterns of unmet needs to your supervisor or program manager.

sources.title: Minnesota Statutes 2025, section 256B.4905 — Home and Community-Based Services Policy Statement
sources.note: Section 256B.4905 sets Minnesota's informed choice policy for home and community-based services, including documentation of each option discussed. Subdivision 3a, Informed decision making, includes "identification of the person's cultural needs and access to culturally responsive services and providers" among the items the process must address for waiver participants.

sources.title: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Office of Minority Health — Cultural and Linguistic Competence (National CLAS Standards)
sources.note: Describes the National CLAS Standards as 15 actionable steps under a principal standard that begins "Provide effective, understandable, and respectful quality care and services."

sources.title: Disability Hub MN
sources.note: Disability Hub MN describes itself as a free statewide resource network that helps people with disabilities solve problems and plan for the future.

sources.title: Yali Pang and Dana V. Yarbrough — The Promising Practice of Cultural Brokering Support with Culturally Diverse Families of Children with Developmental Disabilities, Developmental Disabilities Network Journal (2023)
sources.note: Recommends that providers work closely with families to decide how cultural brokering support is offered and who serves each community.
